newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: New Moldovan leader promises faster reforms.
newsitem.headline: New Moldovan leader promises faster reforms.

text.p: New Moldovan President Petru Lucinschi, sworn into office on Wednesday, promised he would do away with crime and poverty in the former Soviet republic and urged reconciliation with the breakaway Dnestr region.
Lucinschi, elected on December 1, predicted life would soon improve for Moldova's 4.3 million people, made up of 60 percent ethnic Romanians and a large Slav minority.
"Moldova's independence can in no way be considered a joke," he told a news conference after swearing during his inauguration to safeguard the country's independence, unity and territorial integrity.
"I promise that within two years we will have forgotten such phenomenon of today as crime, poverty and wage arrears," Lucinschi told a news conference after his inauguration.
Lucinschi, 56, said he would propose the chairman of the State Audit Chamber, Ion Chubuk, as prime minister. He praised his nominee as a "professional economist and man of principle".

In his inauguration speech, Lucinschi acknowledged 1997 would be a difficult year, "but it could be the last year of acute crisis. We have to remove barricades which have divided society...Only accelerated reforms will stop the crisis."
The new Moldovan leader, a communist apparatchik turned market reformer, defeated incumbent Mircea Snegur in a runoff.
A largely agricultural country sandwiched between Ukraine and Romania, Moldova has won praise from the International Monetary Fund for its reforming zeal, but many citizens remain deep in poverty.

The economic situation is far more dismal in the Dnestr region, where Russian and Ukrainian speakers declared a separate state in 1991 in response to calls by nationalists for a merger with Romania. No country has recognised the self-styled Dnestr Republic.
Most Dnestr residents shunned the Moldovan elections but selected their own leader in separate polls on December 22.

Igor Smirnov, separatist head of the local administration, won another five years in office. He and other leaders failed to attend Lucinschi's inauguration, saying they were too busy forming their local government.
The region, with a population of around 700,000, was Moldova's industrial heartland in Soviet days.

Lucinschi campaigned on a platform of closer ties with Moscow and on Wednesday described Russia as a "strategic partner of great importance". Moldova would have close ties with Russia for centuries, he added.
But he said Moldovan stability could not be guaranteed unless its territory became unified and the 6,000 Russian-led troops still based in Dnestr left the region.

Moldova and Russia, he said, would resume talks next month on withdrawing the troops. Although Russia's parliament had yet to ratify the agreement, he said arms would be removed and troop numbers reduced to 2,500, without mentioning a deadline.
Nationalist calls for a merger between Moldova and Romania, which share a common language and cultural heritage, have all but died out in both countries.

But Lucinschi and Romanian President Emil Constantinescu agreed last month to boost trade ties, improve border crossings and build new bridges across the River Prut, which forms the frontier between the two countries.
